reasoning: Both outputs deliver a working, zero-dependency retry-with-backoff fetcher with a green suite and a self-run mutation check, and the established mutation result confirms neither suite is vacuous (expectation 4 satisfied by both). B wins decisively on the three live dimensions. (1) Red evidence: B retained 12 red logs, 12 green logs and a per-cycle implementation snapshot (work/logs/, work/history/). I verified 06-red.txt shows '[0,0,0,0]' vs '[0,100,300,700]' and 08-red.txt shows the jitter failure, and history/01-after.ts -> 02-after.ts -> 09-after.ts confirms the narrated 'ad-hoc if -> bounded loop -> try/catch loop' restructure actually happened. A narrates equivalent failures in a table with specific messages, which reads credibly, but retains no artifact, so its red loop is unverifiable. (2) Observable behaviour vs implementation coupling: this is the decisive gap, and I tested it rather than trusting either report. A asserts on the arguments and call count of an injected sleep collaborator ('assert.deepEqual(waits, [100,200,400])', 'assert.equal(waits.length, 2)'). B injects a virtual clock whose sleep advances a counter and has the fake transport stamp clock.now() on each request, then asserts on when each request actually reached the server ('offsets(net.requests) === [0,100,300,700]'). I applied a behaviour-preserving refactor to both implementations -- splitting each wait into two half-waits, identical total elapsed delay and identical request schedule. A: 4 of 12 tests broke. B: 0 of 14 broke. A's backoff tests are pinned to how the code waits; B's are pinned to what the server observes. (3) Seam identification: B writes the seams down before testing (a six-row question table), explicitly rejects a standalone retry() helper in favour of the existing fetchJson seam with reasoning, and fakes exactly three system boundaries (network, clock, randomness) with hand-written closures -- no internal collaborator faked. A also avoids heavy mocking (a plain closure transport, not a framework) and tests at fetchJson, so it clears the bar, but it pushes sleep and random into the public RetryOptions type documented as 'Injected for tests', and adds a jitter:false production flag that mainly exists to make assertions deterministic. B additionally covers three behaviours A declined -- connection-level failure, Retry-After, and caller abort -- and kills 7 of 7 mutants to A's 6 of 6. A's genuine wins are secondary: it caught a real bug (a trailing sleep after the final attempt), wrote the named regression test while the bug was still live, and kept its test helper outside test/ so the runner does not pick it up -- B's test/support/fakes.ts does get collected, showing as a spurious 14th passing 'test' on a bare 'node --test' (B's own npm script scopes to one file, so the impact is cosmetic). That hygiene point and A's honest YAGNI restraint do not offset a suite that breaks under a refactor that changes no behaviour.

strengths: Caught a real bug during the loop (unconditional sleep in catch, so the final failed attempt slept before throwing) and wrote the named regression test while the bug was still live
Avoided a mocking framework: a hand-written closure transport with a real call counter
Honestly dropped two candidate tests that passed on first write rather than dressing them up as TDD cycles
Test-directory hygiene: helper placed in test-support/ so Node's runner does not collect it, keeping output pristine
Strong stress test that names real holes, including that realSleep is exercised by nothing and that maxDelayMs=30s is a dead code path at maxAttempts=3
Clear plain-English explanation of what backoff and jitter are for
6 of 6 self-run mutations killed; suite runs 12/12 green in ~92ms
weaknesses: Backoff, cap, no-trailing-wait and jitter tests assert on the arguments and call count of the injected sleep collaborator, testing how the code waits rather than what a caller or server observes
Empirically confirmed coupling: a behaviour-preserving refactor splitting each wait into two half-waits (identical total delay, identical request schedule) broke 4 of A's 12 tests
'assert.equal(waits.length, 2)' is a call-count assertion on a collaborator, the pattern expectation 2 warns against
No red or green logs retained, so the nine narrated red cycles cannot be verified from the artifact
Test seams leak into the production API: sleep and random sit in the public RetryOptions, documented as 'Injected for tests'
The jitter:false flag exists largely to make deterministic assertions possible
No coverage of connection-level abort, Retry-After, or caller cancellation (declined as YAGNI, though A itself names Retry-After as the most likely next requirement)

strengths: Virtual-clock seam: sleep advances a counter and the fake transport stamps clock.now(), so tests assert on when each request actually reached the server -- the thing an outage victim cares about
Verified refactor-resilient: the same behaviour-preserving half-wait refactor that broke 4 of A's tests broke 0 of B's 14
Full red/green evidence retained (work/logs/00-12) plus a per-cycle implementation snapshot (work/history/); I spot-checked 06-red.txt and 08-red.txt and both show the right assertion diff
history/ corroborates the narrated restructure (if status===503 -> bounded loop -> try/catch loop) with no existing assertion changing, which is the claim a seam argument lives or dies on
Seams written down before any test: a six-row question table naming where the tests would change shape, including the explicit choice of fetchJson over a standalone retry() helper
Exactly three boundaries faked (network, clock, randomness); no internal collaborator mocked
Broader production-relevant coverage: connection-level failure, Retry-After honoured over the computed guess, and abort short-circuiting
7 of 7 self-run mutations killed, each mapped to the single test that notices
Caught and reported a real suite defect mid-run: three tests were falling through to setTimeout and really sleeping, pushing the suite to 897ms before the virtual clock brought it to 84ms

Unusually candid stress test: discloses that tsc --noEmit was never run, that random:()=>1 is a value Math.random cannot return, that a malformed JSON body is wrongly treated as transient (found by reading code, not by a test), and that POST replay is unguarded
Directly answers the 'eleven cycles is theatre' critique with the three things the loop surfaced that writing it in one go would not have
weaknesses: test/support/fakes.ts is collected by a bare 'node --test' and shows as a spurious 14th passing entry; the npm script scopes to one file, so impact is cosmetic, but A noticed this class of pollution and B did not
random: () => 1 pins a boundary Math.random never reaches (self-flagged)
FetcherDeps mixes boundaries (transport, clock, random) with policy (retry) -- self-flagged and deferred to review rather than fixed
The abort check runs after the in-flight request resolves, so it prevents further attempts rather than cancelling the current one
Retry-After and abort arguably exceed the literal ask, though each was driven by its own red test
systemClock, the path that runs in production, is exercised by no test (self-flagged; A has the same hole)
